title: Exploring Student Experiences and Digital Inequities in Asynchronous Computer Science Education: A Mixed-Methods Study
author: Armando Amador, Saadia Lgarch
description: Digital inclusion has become a critical factor in asynchronous online learning, particularly as higher education increasingly relies on digital platforms for instruction. This mixed-methods study examined how computer science students experience digital inclusion and exclusion in asynchronous environments at Hostos Community College, a Hispanic-serving institution. Survey data from 36 undergraduates in four asynchronous Computer Science courses were analyzed to examine access, digital skills, home environments, and interaction design. Results showed that 72% of students worked, 61% had family responsibilities, and 22% experienced technical issues. Schedule management had the strongest correlation with satisfaction (r = +0.72). Sixty-seven percent used AI tools, primarily ChatGPT, for concept explanation and code support. Findings identify flexibility, interaction, feedback, and meaningful technology use as central dimensions of asynchronous CS learning and suggest course-design strategies for strengthening digital inclusion.

title: Exploring the use of generative AI in postgraduate GP training: a qualitative study of resident doctors’ experiences and perceptions
author: Gabriele Tankard, Jiawen Dong
description: Abstract Background The use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasing across healthcare, with existing research demonstrating its potential value and applications in medical education and clinical practice. However, less is known about how general practice resident doctors (GPRs), who have a unique position as both learners and practicing clinicians, are using generative AI in their everyday work. Methods This qualitative study, conducted within a post-positivist paradigm, explored the use of generative AI by GPRs, and their perceptions of its benefits, risks and training needs. Five semi-structured focus groups were conducted with 16 GPRs from the Northern region. Results The data were analysed thematically, and four themes were identified: ‘AI as a response to workload and time pressure’, ‘AI as a clinical cognitive aid and educational support’, ‘Safe use of AI requires professional judgement and accountability’ and ‘Preparing for an AI-enabled future’. Participants used AI to improve efficiency with repetitive, admin-heavy tasks, such as documentation, written communication and portfolio development. author: Rani Siti Fitriani, Saima Hasin Roompa
description: Online and blended courses can widen opportunities for participation in library and information science education, but delivery mode alone does not explain what students learn. This narrative review examines how course design connects flexible access with the development and assessment of professional capabilities. It brings literature on blended learning, constructive alignment and self-regulation into dialogue with selected recent studies of responsible AI use, teacher learning and personalization. The analysis distinguishes participation, perceived confidence and demonstrated competence, while treating evidence from other disciplines as contextual. A proposed instructional cycle links preparation, guided practice, feedback and independent application. Illustrative designs address metadata creation, reference consultation, digital collection curation and information literacy instruction. The review specifies how each activity can generate evidence of learning and how optional AI assistance should be bounded and disclosed. title: AI-Enabled Early Warning and Intervention Systems for Student Success in Higher Education: An Evidence-Informed, Human-Centered Architecture for Predictive Identification, Timely Intervention, and Institutional Learning
author: Asrat Amnie
description: Higher education institutions increasingly hold rich streams of academic, learning-management-system (LMS), engagement, and student-support data capable of revealing academic difficulty before withdrawal or stop-out becomes irreversible. Advances in learning analytics and machine learning create an opportunity to shift student-success practice from reactive to earlier, more individualized support. Yet prediction is not intervention, and algorithmic accuracy is not educational effectiveness. This integrative, evidence-informed manuscript synthesizes peer-reviewed research on predictive analytics, early warning systems, intervention effectiveness, privacy, equity, and human-centered artificial intelligence (AI) to argue that the most defensible model is an AI-enabled early warning and intervention system rather than an AI-operated one, in which AI augments professional judgment and student agency rather than replacing them. title: DESIGNING CYBER-RESILIENT SECONDARY SCHOOLS IN INDONESIA: INTEGRATING PHISHING LITERACY, DATA PRIVACY PROTECTION, AND CYBER INCIDENT RESPONSE

author: Syafar Faisal, Halimah Husain
description: Secondary schools increasingly rely on digital learning platforms, messaging, and student information systems, but cyber-safety instruction often prioritizes awareness over coordinated prevention, response, and recovery. Objective: This article develops a context-sensitive framework for Indonesian junior secondary, senior secondary, and vocational schools by integrating phishing literacy, personal-data protection, and cyber incident response. Methods: A targeted integrative synthesis of peer-reviewed work on adolescent digital resilience, privacy education, phishing interventions, and organizational security informed a design-science conceptual artifact. Requirements were organized into learner, staff, governance, and response domains. Results: The proposed School Cyber-Resilience Learning and Response (SCR-LR) framework connects three instructional strands with school responsibilities and six incident-management stages. title: The Tech-Assisted Educator: Integrating Digital Tools with Core Pedagogical Strategies in English Language Teaching
publisher: International Journal of Social Science and Human Research
author: Afet Guliyeva
description: Digital technology now forms part of everyday English language teaching, but its educational value depends on how teachers connect each tool to a clear language objective. This paper examines how digital tools can support established ELT pedagogy through the TPACK framework, communicative and task-based approaches, mobile-assisted language learning, self-regulated learning, digital assessment, and artificial intelligence. The review draws on peer-reviewed research, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and established academic books. Across these areas, the evidence points to a consistent pattern: technology is most useful when it extends purposeful practice, interaction, feedback, and learner autonomy rather than when it becomes the focus of the lesson. Recent studies report positive effects for several language outcomes, especially speaking, writing, vocabulary, and grammar, although results vary across learners, tools, and contexts. The analysis therefore places the teacher at the centre of digital ELT as a pedagogical decision-maker who selects, adapts, evaluates, and sometimes rejects technology according to learner needs. title: Researchers’ expectations of higher education teachers’ roles in AI-enhanced education by 2035
author: Fabio Batista Mota, Luiza Amara Maciel Braga
description: Abstract Background The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence in higher education has outpaced governance, raising uncertainty about how academic teaching roles will change. Objective This study examines researchers’ expectations for how higher education teaching roles may evolve by 2035 amid the continued integration of artificial intelligence. Methods We conducted a global online survey of 538 authors of peer-reviewed articles on artificial intelligence and education. Participants rated 15 future-oriented statements on a 5-point agreement Likert scale. Results Respondents anticipated automation of routine teaching tasks, a limited likelihood of broad teacher replacement, and a shift toward facilitation and preparation of students for artificial intelligence-rich workplaces. They did not anticipate fully artificial intelligence-delivered instruction and flagged risks. Conclusion Respondents expect higher education to move toward human-artificial intelligence teams and a reconfigured, rather than replaced, teaching role by 2035, centered on guidance, feedback, ethics, and socio-emotional support. Such a transition may require institutions to redesign roles and evaluation system

title: Illocutionary Changes and Student Uptake of Generative AI Feedback in Public Service Announcement Script Revision
author: Rawinda Fitrotul Mualafina, Siti Ulfiyani
description: Students who revise a persuasive script with the help of generative AI may change how the text sounds without changing what it asks the audience to do. This study examines that difference in the closing messages of public service announcement (PSA) scripts written by 24 students in an Indonesian university course in February 2026. For each script, the closing of the initial and final versions was extracted as written and coded for representative and directive functions following Searle (1976). Each pair was then classified as unchanged, changed in wording only, or changed in function. The first coding was prepared with AI assistance, and a second author coded independently; the two coders agreed on 85% of decisions (Cohen's κ = 0.72) and resolved their differences through discussion. Most closings already asked the audience to act in the initial version (21 of 24). Three closings remained unchanged, 19 changed only in wording, and two gained a function, one of which was a judgment call. Because the AI's suggestions and the students' prompts were not coded and no revision without AI was compared, the study cannot determine what the AI contributed; it describes one class only.

author: Thien Tran, Khang Duong
description: Abstract Without thoughtful instructional design, the transition to industrial-standard platforms in educational robotics can impose substantial cognitive load on novice engineering students, hindering sustained knowledge construction and equitable skill development. Resource-constrained institutions often struggle to deliver design-based learning in these technical contexts. Industry-grade simulators are costly and complex, while open-source alternatives remain code-centric, exacerbating cognitive overload for novice learners and instructors. To widen access and provide smart pedagogical scaffolding, we introduce the Graphical Open-Source Platform (GOSP), a ROS-Blender digital learning environment. GOSP lowers the coding burden by putting visual design, simulation, and safe experimentation first for manipulator tasks. To establish evidence-based principles for its integration, we investigate GOSP and ABB RobotStudio (RS) utilising a two-group crossover design-based learning (DBL) workshop and a partial-overlap remake round ( $$N=16$$ ). title: The Relationship Between AI Writing Engagement and Argumentative Writing Skills of BS Students at a Pakistani University
author: Mahnoor Fatima, Shahida Naz
description: Artificial intelligence (AI) writing tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, and QuillBot have rapidly become part of undergraduate writing practice, yet it remains unclear whether students' engagement with these tools is reflected in their independently assessed writing ability. This quantitative, cross-sectional correlational study examined the relationship between AI writing engagement and the argumentative writing performance of Bachelor of Science (BS) students at a Pakistani university. Seventy-five undergraduates (62.7% female) at Government College University Faisalabad completed an adapted 19-item AI Writing Engagement Questionnaire assessing AI Knowledge (9 items) and perceived Writing Impact (10 items), and then wrote a timed, unassisted IELTS Academic Writing Task 2 argumentative essay scored using analytic IELTS criteria. Descriptive statistics and Pearson product–moment correlations were computed in R. Students reported moderately high AI Knowledge (M = 3.48, SD = 0.62) and Writing Impact (M = 3.59, SD = 0.70), whereas their argumentative writing clustered in the mid-band range (M = 5.53, SD = 0.90). title: PEMETAAN TREN PENELITIAN COOPERATIVE LEARNING DALAM PENDIDIKAN: ANALISIS BIBLIOMETRIK TAHUN 2021 - 2026
author: Ria Yurliza Sapitri, Afif Rahman Riyanda
description: This study aims to map research trends in Cooperative Learning in education through a bibliometric analysis of 159 Scopus-indexed publications from 2021 to 2026. The analysis uses the PRISMA framework and VOSviewer software to examine publication trends, keyword patterns, and geographical distribution. The findings show that publications peaked in 2022 with 32 articles and reached their lowest point in 2023 with 20 articles. Keyword mapping identified four clusters covering cooperative learning, student interaction, educational technology, and online learning. Dominant keywords include cooperative learning, students, teaching, engineering education, and e-learning. Spain contributed the highest number of publications (37 articles), followed by the United States (26 articles) and China (25 articles). The findings highlight opportunities for further research on individual participation, technology integration, and the implementation of Cooperative Learning across diverse educational contexts.

title: Perceived Functionality of School  Governance Councils in Small and Medium  Public Elementary and Secondary Schools in the Schools Division of Ilocos Sur: Basis for a  Context-Responsive Enhancement Framework
publisher: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology
author: Ghizelle G. Balao
description: School Governance Councils (SGCs) are intended to provide a structure through which school stakeholders can participate in governance, offer feedback, and support school improvement. However, the existence of a council does not by itself demonstrate that members understand their roles, receive adequate institutional support, or sustain council activities over time. This review examines literature and policy relevant to the perceived functionality of SGCs in small and medium public elementary and secondary schools in the Schools Division of Ilocos Sur. It brings together international research on school governance, governing-body relationships, community-based school management, and school autonomy with Philippine studies on SGC implementation, stakeholder engagement, and School-Based Management (SBM). The literature points to three connected areas: member capacity, operational and institutional support, and continuity and sustainability. Direct Philippine evidence on SGC implementation identifies funding, training, scheduling, commitment, role clarity, and stakeholder engagement as continuing concerns. title: AI-POWERED PERSONALIZED LEARNING: OPPORTUNITIES AND CHALLENGES FOR STUDENT-CENTRED HIGHER EDUCATION
publisher: PUPIL: International Journal of Teaching, Education and Learning
author: Dharminder Singh
description: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education by enabling learning environments that can respond more effectively to the diverse needs, abilities, preferences, and learning progress of individual students. Among these developments, AI-powered personalized learning has emerged as a significant approach for moving beyond conventional one-size-fits-all models towards more flexible and student-centred education. By using intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, learning analytics, recommendation systems, and Generative AI, higher education institutions can potentially provide individualized learning pathways, real-time feedback, targeted academic support, and learning resources suited to students’ varying levels of knowledge and achievement. This paper examines the opportunities and challenges associated with AI-powered personalized learning and considers its implications for the development of student-centred higher education. title: The Influence of Animated Video Education on Knowledge Levels and Behavior Prevention of Diabetes Mellitus in School Children
author: Gian Hawara, Veri
description: Background: Diabetes mellitus among children continues to increase due to lifestyle changesand low levels of health literacy. Innovative educational media are needed to improveknowledge and to shape preventive behaviors from an early age.Purpose: To evaluate the effect of digital animated video–based education on the level ofknowledge and diabetes mellitus prevention behaviors among elementary school students atMI Raudhatul Muta’aliminMethods: This quantitative study employed a pre-experimental one-group pretest–posttestdesign involving 54 students. The intervention consisted of digital animated video education.Data were analyzed using the Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test.Results: The mean knowledge score increased from 4.61 to 10.30 with a p-value= 0.000 (p <0.05). The behavior score increased from 21.07 to 26.17 with a p-value = 0.000 (p<0.05).Conclusions: Digital animated video–based education is effective in improving knowledge andpreventive behaviors related to diabetes mellitus among elementary school children.

title: Affective drivers of generative AI acceptance in higher education: a UTAUT extension across on-campus and distance learning
author: Mareike Mueller, Evelyn Kaestner
description: Purpose This study aims to examine the drivers of students’ intention to intensify generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) use in higher education, focusing on the incremental explanatory value of Affective Evaluation and differences between on-campus and distance-learning students. Design/methodology/approach Building on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), the study analyzes survey data from 502 students at a German university of applied sciences. Hierarchical regression analyses, group comparisons and moderation analyses are used to examine predictor–intention relationships and the role of study mode. Findings The UTAUT-based model explained approximately 62% of the variance in Intention to Intensify GenAI Use. Affective Evaluation contributed significant incremental explanatory power and showed the largest standardized coefficient, alongside significant effects of Performance Expectancy and Social Influence. Distance-learning students reported higher intention than on-campus students, although the effect was small. title: Understanding the potential role of GenAI and knowledge governance in the higher education sector through knowledge governance theory
author: Xie Xiaojuan, Muhammad Azfar Anwar
description: Purpose This study aims to investigate how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) knowledge workflow capabilities influence community knowledge governance (CKG) and community knowledge sharing (CKS) within higher education communities, through the mediating mechanisms of knowledge digitization and knowledge legitimacy. Scales were adapted from validated instruments in prior knowledge management, AI capability and academic behavior research, ensuring reliability and construct validity across all measured variables. description: The following chapter derives from research shaped by the COVID-19 pandemic. Although its main aim was not to discuss the impacts of the pandemic, the context in which it occurred allows us to ask: what do the changes brought about by pandemic-related restrictions reveal about the social mediations of our participants’ out-of-school study practices? To address this question, we employed a theory-generating methodology, supported by questionnaires that provided contextual elements of these practices and by explicitation interviews that allowed a deeper analysis. These interviews provide the main data analyzed. Tim Ingold’s concept of enskillment and Bernard Charlot’s concept of the relationship with knowledge structured the analyses conducted. The data originate from a comparative study involving three California universities and one Brazilian public university. We argue that the main issue faced by the U.S. interviewees was de-enskillment, a broadening of the Ingoldian concept. Meanwhile, among the Brazilian participants, it was possible to shed light on inequalities between public high school students and private high school attendees. title: From Ideation to Implementation
publisher: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
author: Brad Ost, Bryan A. Briones
description: This chapter examines how the Atlanta University Center Robert W. Woodruff Library developed an AI Sandbox to support responsible, equitable, and innovative adoption of generative AI across its three Historically Black Colleges and Universities consortial partner campuses; Clark Atlanta University, Morehouse College and Spelman College. Framed within the evolving and expanding role of academic libraries, it confirms that libraries are uniquely situated to address the challenges of AI access, data privacy, governance, and information literacy while also advancing research, teaching innovation, and student success. The chapter traces the sandbox's conceptualization, partnership development, governance structuring, environmental scanning, and strategic planning, highlighting some examples of lessons learned throughout the process. It demonstrates how the AI Sandbox enhanced the AUC Woodruff Library's mission by linking emerging technologies with existing research support, digital scholarship, and ethical information practices to create a sustainable model for AI-enabled scholarship.

title: Critical Thinking in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
publisher: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
author: avram anderson, Ahmed Alwan
description: Artificial intelligence (AI) has had and will continue to have, an unprecedented impact on higher education. Yet the integration of AI literacy into postsecondary curricula remains rare and inconsistent. Academic librarians, due to their expertise in information literacy and interdisciplinary collaboration, are uniquely positioned to address this gap. This chapter presents a case study of a credit-bearing AI literacy course housed within the academic library at CSUN. The course was designed not only to introduce students to AI but to support the development of epistemic agency, allowing them to critically evaluate AI-generated information, interrogate algorithmic bias, and navigate an AI-mediated information environment. Grounded in the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Students, the Council of Europe's three-dimensional model of AI literacy and ACRL Framework for Information Literacy for Higher Education, the course emphasizes the practical and human dimensions of AI literacy and provides a pedagogical framework that academic librarians can adapt across instructional formats.

This paper treats the difficulty as conceptual. A systematic search of 1,373 records from OpenAlex and four from a targeted Chinese search yielded 46 studies published between 2017 and 2026, coded for design, technology role, POA stage and outcome. The corpus is deliberately mixed and is not a set of 46 instances: eight are POA sources written before generative tools existed, twenty-six combine POA with AI, ten examine AI in second language reading without POA, and two are reviews. A quantitative approach with a one-group pretest–posttest design was employed. The participants were 54 students from Universitas Tomakaka, comprising 22 Mechanical Engineering students and 32 Civil Engineering students, selected using total sampling. Data were collected using a 20-item multiple-choice test and analyzed descriptively and using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. title: Reclaiming the Civic Mission of Higher Education Through Social Entrepreneurship and Experiential Assessment
author: Sein Tin, Lachhuman Gurung
description: Higher education is facing a compounding legitimacy crisis driven by neoliberal marketisation, generative artificial intelligence, and public doubt about the value of degrees. This chapter argues that assessment is a significant yet underexplored mechanism through which neoliberal values are reproduced: standardised, output-driven individual assessment narrows curricula, marginalises civic and ethical learning, and reinforces educational inequalities, while AI exposes the limitations of these models. In response, the chapter develops the Civic-Embedded Assessment Framework (CEAF), grounded in civic university, experiential learning, student integration, and social entrepreneurship theories. The CEAF proposes four interdependent pillars: social value creation, authentic knowledge application, community engagement, and student identity development. title: AI-Augmented Research Support for Commerce Collections
publisher: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
author: Deepak D.
description: This chapter analyses a case study of the systematic use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in re-engineering the research-support service for its commerce collection in an Indian management institute library. The study follows the evolution of a library from reactive support via reference work to proactive, data-driven research partnership based on a single-site case-study design across two academic years: 2023-24 and 2024-25. The five-layer AI tool stack—presentation, AI service, knowledge, infrastructure and governance—is introduced alongside a six-step augmented research workflow using generative AI assistants, retrieval-augmented chatbots, automated summarisation of results, citation bots for tutorial creation and text-mining services.The use of pre- and post-implementation usage data, qualitative feedback, and an adoption-maturity model illustrates measurable improvements in discovery efficiency, citation accuracy, and faculty research output.

title: Inner Development Goals and Collective Social-Emotional Health in Higher Education Institutions
publisher: Cultivating Collective Socio-Emotional Well-Being in Organizations
author: Yuliya Shtaltovna
description: This chapter examines collective socio-emotional health through the lens of the Inner Development Goals (IDG). Moving beyond individual resilience, it argues that socio-emotional health is an organizational capability shaped by relational infrastructure, leadership norms, communication cultures, institutional practices, and technological conditions. The chapter positions the IDG dimensions of Being, Thinking, Relating, Collaborating, and Acting as a framework for understanding how inner capacities become collective practices that support trust, psychological safety, empathy, shared meaning, and responsible action. Drawing on selected IDG cases from the Casebook of IDG Implementation into Higher Education, it illustrates how relational well-being can be intentionally designed in higher education organizations and communities. The chapter offers recommendations for researchers, educators, leaders, policy makers, social innovators, and well-being professionals seeking to cultivate emotionally healthy collectives in an age of complexity, artificial intelligence, and human sustainability.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Journalism
publisher: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
author: Andleeb Raza, Rahul Kumar
description: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping journalism through automated content creation, data analysis, and personalized news distribution. While it enhances efficiency, AI also raises profound ethical concerns, including algorithmic bias, deepfake-driven misinformation, and the erosion of editorial accountability. This chapter explores AI's dual impact, emphasizing how algorithmic gatekeeping and synthetic media threaten media literacy and democratic discourse. Case studies illustrate how filter bubbles and computational propaganda exploit AI to distort public perception. A pilot study in Jammu and Kashmir reveals high media literacy among youth (mean: 3.98/5), despite regional vulnerabilities, demonstrating education's vital role in building resilience. The chapter advocates for comprehensive media literacy programs, regulatory frameworks to ensure algorithmic transparency, and newsroom policies that maintain human oversight. Addressing these challenges is essential to harness AI's potential while safeguarding journalism's integrity and democratic values in digital landscape.

title: Applications of artificial intelligence in microbiology education
author: Sherab Pelmo, Vandana Gulati
description: Microbiology underpins understanding of infectious disease, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), biotechnology, public health, food, agriculture and environmental sustainability. Although attention to artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has centred largely on generative tools, a broader range of AI technologies is creating opportunities across microbiology education. This article outlines applications in personalised learning, laboratory skills, diagnostics and image analysis, epidemiology and AMR education, drawing from contemporary literature. It distinguishes microbiology-specific evidence of educational benefit from professional exposure and evidence from other fields and suggests approaches educators can try. Potential benefits include engagement, conceptual understanding, accessibility and professional readiness, alongside challenges such as data privacy, digital inequity, environmental cost and overreliance on AI.

title: STUDENT EXPERIENCE OF AI IN LAW ASSESSMENT: AN EXPLORATORY STUDY
author: Benedict Sheehy, Juan Diaz-Granados
description: Legal education faces particular challenges as a result of the wide dissemination of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI). GenAI can produce outputs that appear to challenge the work of licensed lawyers. This challenge requires educators and students to be knowledgeable about the powers and limitations of GenAI. This article presents a study of student experimentation with GenAI aimed at developing that knowledge. The experiment incorporated GenAI’s drafting capabilities into an assessment item required in a core subject, Tort Law. The article presents the responses and reflections of the students on the GenAI exercise and provokes further thinking about student experience, uses of and potential with GenAI in legal education. It argues that the most promising pedagogical response is neither blanket prohibition nor uncritical adoption, but a structured use-and-critique model in which students engage directly with GenAI and then evaluate its adequacy against disciplinary and professional standards.

title: From Affordance to Coupling: Reconstructing Foreign Language Pedagogy through an AI-Enabled Production-Oriented Approach
author: Xuan Sun
description: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now a routine presence in foreign language classrooms, yet the gap between what the technology can do and what it actually teaches remains poorly theorised. This paper argues that the gap is structural, and that it is best analysed at the level of the pedagogic move. Taking the Production-Oriented Approach (POA) as its anchor, the paper identifies three chronic constraints in POA practice: the cost of evaluating student output, the difficulty of matching input to diagnosed gaps, and the delay between production and feedback. It then proposes the construct of an AI-enabled Production-Oriented Approach (AI-POA), which frames AI as a change in the resourcing and pacing of an existing cycle. Three affordances of generative AI (generative, dialogic, evaluative) are specified, together with four conditions under which they couple with instruction: goal alignment, temporal placement, cognitive appropriateness and teacher control.
